[Section] Experiment Results on KP20k Absent Subset
[source_id=81] Generating absent keyphrases on scientific publication datasets is a rather challenging problem. Existing studies often achieve seemingly good performance by measuring recall on tens and sometimes hundreds of keyphrases produced by exhaustive decoding with a large beam size — thus completely ignoring precision.
[source_id=82] We report the models' R@10/50 scores on the absent portion of five scientific paper datasets in Table TABREF48 to be in line with previous studies.
[source_id=83] The absent keyphrase prediction highly prefers recall-oriented models, therefore CopyRNN with beam size of 200 is innately proper for this task setting. Howerer, from the results we observe that with the help of exhaustive decoding and diverse mechanisms, INLINEFORM0 is able to perform comparably to CopyRNN model, and it generally works better for top predictions. Even though the trend of models' performance somewhat matches what we observe on the present data, we argue that it is hard to compare different models' performance on such scale. We argue that StackEx is better testbeds for absent keyphrase generation.
child_qasper_evidence_texts: Generating absent keyphrases on scientific publication datasets is a rather challenging problem. Existing studies often achieve seemingly good performance by measuring recall on tens and sometimes hundreds of keyphrases produced by exhaustive decoding with a large beam size — thus completely ignoring precision.
We report the models' R@10/50 scores on the absent portion of five scientific paper datasets in Table TABREF48 to be in line with previous studies.

The absent keyphrase prediction highly prefers recall-oriented models, therefore CopyRNN with beam size of 200 is innately proper for this task setting. Howerer, from the results we observe that with the help of exhaustive decoding and diverse mechanisms, INLINEFORM0 is able to perform comparably to CopyRNN model, and it generally works better for top predictions. Even though the trend of models' performance somewhat matches what we observe on the present data, we argue that it is hard to compare different models' performance on such scale. We argue that StackEx is better testbeds for absent keyphrase generation.
